item.title: 1-Month Biology Olympiad Study Plan
item.description:
Who this plan is for

Students with solid foundations who need a structured final ramp-up. You’ve already studied the core syllabus – cell biology, genetics, physiology – and you’ve done at least a few practice papers. If you’ve never opened Campbell Biology, this timeframe won’t get you there. Be honest with yourself and set realistic goals.

This plan is also the right fit for students who qualified for INBO from NSEB, or for USABO Semifinal from the Open, and have 4-6 weeks before the next stage.

What you can realistically achieve

Paper-level fluency on topics you already partially know, sharper exam technique, and a clearer map of your strengths and weaknesses going into the exam. You won’t learn new material in depth – but you can significantly improve your performance on material you already understand by practicing retrieval under timed conditions.

Week-by-week breakdown

Week 1: Diagnostic and priority map

Day 1-2: Full diagnostic paper. Take a complete past paper (BiOrchive) under timed exam conditions. No notes, no breaks, strict timing.

Day 3: Error analysis. Go through every wrong answer and categorize:

Category Count What it means
Knowledge gap (didn’t know the fact/mechanism) ___ These topics need focused revision
Reasoning error (knew the fact, applied it wrong) ___ These topics need more practice problems, not more reading
Reading error (misread the question) ___ Slow down on “not,” “except,” “which of the following is false” questions
Time pressure (didn’t reach the question) ___ Practice pacing strategy

Day 4-7: Priority revision. Rank your knowledge gaps by frequency across the paper. The top 3-4 topics that cost you the most marks are your revision priorities for weeks 2 and 3. Go back to your textbook for these specific sections – read, then immediately test yourself from memory.

Week 2: Focused revision + paper practice

Alternate days:

Day type Activity Duration
Revision day Deep study on your #1 or #2 weak topic. Read the relevant textbook chapter, then test yourself with Question Bank questions on that topic. 2-3 hrs
Paper day Timed past paper. Afterward, quick error check – are you still losing marks on the same topics, or have they improved? 2-3 hrs

Target: 3 revision days + 2 paper days this week. After each paper, update your error tracking. If a topic improves, move on to the next priority. If it doesn’t, spend another revision day on it.

Week 3: Intensify paper practice

4-5 papers this week. One every other day at minimum.

By now, your revision priorities should be sharpening. The topics that cost you marks in week 1 should be improving. New weak spots may have emerged – address them in your revision sessions between papers.

Between papers:

  • Review errors (30-45 min max – don’t re-read the whole paper)
  • Targeted review of any topic that cost you 3+ marks on the paper you just did
  • No new textbook chapters – this is refinement, not new learning

Time management focus: Are you finishing papers with time to spare, or running out? If you’re running out:

  • Practice skipping questions you’re unsure about and marking them for return
  • Set a per-question time budget (e.g., 90 seconds per statement on IBO theory)
  • Practice the “two-pass” strategy: answer everything you’re confident about first, then go back to uncertain questions

Week 4: Exam simulation and rest

Days 1-3: Two full mocks under strict exam conditions. Time it exactly. No notes. Simulate the real experience as closely as possible.

Days 4-5: Light review of any remaining weak spots from the last two mocks. Keep it to 1-2 hours per day maximum.

Days 6-7: Rest. Seriously. Sleep well. Don’t cram. The evidence consistently shows that sleep consolidation matters more than last-minute review at this stage.

What NOT to do in the last month

Don’t start a new textbook. If you haven’t read Alberts by now, starting it this week won’t help. Use the references you already have.

Don’t try to learn a completely new topic from scratch. If you’ve never studied bioinformatics, spending a week on it now means less time on topics you actually know and can score on. Accept the marks you’ll lose on unfamiliar topics and maximize your score on familiar ones.

Don’t do papers without reviewing them. A paper you don’t analyze is wasted practice. The error analysis is where learning happens, not the attempt itself.

Don’t study 8+ hours a day. Diminishing returns are real. 3-4 focused hours per day with good sleep beats 8 exhausted hours.

Daily rhythm

Fifteen to twenty hours a week, roughly two to three focused hours a day. Weekend blocks of four to five hours for full paper attempts.

Component Hours/week
Past-paper attempts (timed) 6-8
Error analysis and review 3-4
Targeted topic revision 4-6
Rest and unfocused review 2-3

Resources

You shouldn’t be adding new resources at this stage. Use:

  • BiOrchive for past papers (the core of this plan)
  • Question Bank for drilling specific weak topics
  • Study Dashboard for tracking your mastery trends across attempts
  • Whatever textbooks you’ve already been using – as reference for lookups only
  • Your own notes from earlier study

Adding new resources this late usually hurts more than it helps – it fragments your attention and creates the illusion of progress without actual retrieval practice.

item.title: 1-Year Biology Olympiad Study Plan
item.description:
Who this plan is for

Students who already have school-biology foundations (AP Biology, CBSE/ICSE Class 12, or equivalent) and can put in eight to ten hours a week for a full year. This is the default plan for serious olympiad prep – enough time to cover everything without cutting corners, but not enough time to waste on topics you already understand.

What you can realistically achieve

Full syllabus coverage plus solid past-paper competence. Strong INBO/USABO showing likely. IBO qualification depends on your system’s pathway and your peers, but you’ll be well-prepared for whatever selection process comes next.

Phase 1: Foundations (months 1-3)

Month Section What to focus on Weekly hours
1 Cell & Molecular Biology and Biochemistry Enzyme kinetics, metabolic pathways, membrane transport, signal transduction. You likely know the basics from school – push to mechanism-level understanding. 8-10
2 Genetics Mendelian inheritance with extensions, then molecular genetics (gene regulation, molecular techniques). Practice linkage problems – they require a different skill than reading about genetics. 8-10
3 Animal Physiology (first half) Cardiovascular, respiratory, nervous system. Start Silverthorn if Campbell’s depth isn’t enough for practice questions. 8-10

Primary resources: Campbell Biology as the baseline. When Campbell’s explanation of enzyme kinetics or signal transduction leaves you unable to answer IBO-level questions, pick up Alberts or Lehninger for those specific chapters.

First diagnostic past paper at the end of month 2. Don’t wait until you’ve covered everything. Score doesn’t matter – the point is to learn what IBO questions actually look like and calibrate your expectations.

Phase 2: Broaden (months 4-7)

Month Section What to focus on
4 Finish Animal Physiology + Animal Anatomy Renal, endocrine, immune system. Comparative anatomy across major phyla.
5 Plant Physiology + Plant Anatomy Photosynthesis (PS I/II, C3/C4/CAM), phytohormones, water transport, root/stem/leaf anatomy. Don’t skip this – plant biology is 25-30% of IBO.
6 Ecology + Evolution Population dynamics, community ecology, population genetics (Hardy-Weinberg quantitative problems), speciation.
7 Ethology + Bioinformatics Behavioral ecology, mating systems. BLAST basics, sequence alignment, phylogenetic tree reading.

Weekly rhythm: 8-10 hours. Three concept sessions (2 hrs each) plus one longer weekend session (2-3 hrs) for past-paper practice or revision.

Past papers from month 4 onward: One paper every two weeks. After each paper, track which topics cost you marks. This feeds your revision priorities in Phase 3.

Textbook upgrades during this phase: Add subject-specific references for your weakest areas:

  • Scoring below 50% on animal physiology questions? Add Silverthorn.
  • Plant physiology questions feel alien? Add Taiz for the relevant chapters.
  • Linkage problems consistently wrong? Add Griffiths’ genetics chapter on mapping.

Phase 3: Practice and refine (months 8-12)

Months Focus Cadence
8-9 Practical sections and gap-filling One past paper per week plus targeted revision on persistent weak areas
10-11 Intensive paper practice Two papers per week. Full timed conditions. Detailed error analysis after each.
12 Exam simulation Full papers every 2-3 days. Review between papers. Focus on time management and accuracy under pressure.

Error analysis protocol: For every wrong answer, identify the type:

Error type What it means What to do
Knowledge gap You didn’t know the fact or mechanism Go back to the relevant textbook section and re-study
Reasoning error You knew the fact but applied it wrong Practice more questions on that topic – the knowledge is there but not fluent
Reading error You misread the question or missed a qualifier Practice reading questions more carefully; slow down on “not” and “except” questions

The Study Dashboard automates much of this tracking if you submit your attempts to the leaderboard.

Progress checkpoints

Month Checkpoint Target
2 First diagnostic paper Any score (calibration only)
5 Full paper mock 45-55%
8 Full paper mock 60-70%
11 Full paper mock 70-80%
12 Pre-exam mock 75%+

What to skip

Move on from any subtopic once you get it, even if you feel you could go deeper. A year isn’t enough for research-level depth on every subtopic. The goal is solid understanding of mechanisms across the full syllabus, not exhaustive mastery of any one area.

Resources

  • Campbell Biology as the foundation throughout
  • Subject-specific books (Alberts, Lehninger, Silverthorn, Taiz) for weak areas as identified by practice papers
  • Past papers from month 2 onward
  • Question Bank for targeted drilling
  • Study Dashboard for mastery tracking
  • Full graded book list on the Study Resources page

item.title: 2-Year Biology Olympiad Study Plan
item.description:
Who this plan is for

Anyone from complete beginner to school-biology level who has genuinely committed two years and can put in five to eight hours a week consistently. This is the runway for building real depth – not just coverage, but the kind of understanding where you can answer questions you’ve never seen before because you know the mechanisms, not just the facts.

What you can realistically achieve

Full mastery of the IBO syllabus, competitive standing at INBO/USABO level, and a fair shot at IBO qualification if your national system supports it. Two years gives you something shorter plans can’t: the time to re-study topics after your first pass, which is where real mastery happens.

Phase 1: Foundations (months 1-7)

These are the highest-frequency exam topics. Get them solid before moving on.

Months Section What to focus on Primary resource
1-3 Cell & Molecular Biology and Biochemistry Cell structure, membrane transport, enzyme kinetics, metabolic pathways (glycolysis, Krebs, ox-phos, photosynthesis), signal transduction Campbell Biology (bridge); Alberts Ch. 1-15 when Campbell isn’t deep enough
4-5 Genetics Mendelian inheritance with extensions, linkage mapping, gene regulation (lac/trp operons, eukaryotic), molecular techniques Campbell; Griffiths for linkage problems
6-7 Start Animal Physiology Cardiovascular, respiratory, nervous system basics Campbell; begin Silverthorn

Weekly rhythm: 5-6 hours. Three sessions: two concept-learning (1.5 hrs each), one problem-solving (1.5 hrs). The problem-solving session should use end-of-chapter questions from your textbook, not just re-reading notes.

How to know you’re ready to move on: After finishing a section, do a self-quiz from memory – list the key mechanisms, draw the major pathways, explain the cause-and-effect chains. If you can do this without looking at notes, you’re solid. If not, spend another week on the gaps before moving forward.

Phase 2: Core systems (months 8-14)

Months Section What to focus on Primary resource
8-9 Finish Animal Physiology + Animal Anatomy Renal physiology, endocrine, immune system, comparative anatomy across phyla Silverthorn; Hickman for comparative anatomy
10-11 Plant Anatomy + Plant Physiology Root/stem/leaf anatomy, photosynthesis at PS I/II level, C3/C4/CAM, phytohormones, water potential Campbell; Taiz for mechanism-level plant physiology
12-14 Ecology, Ethology, Evolution Population dynamics, community ecology, behavioral ecology, population genetics (Hardy-Weinberg), speciation Campbell; dedicated ecology text if needed

Weekly rhythm: 6-8 hours. You’re covering more sections now, so add a fourth session on weekends for broader revision of Phase 1 material. Don’t let Cell Biology and Genetics decay while you study physiology.

Bring in past papers at month 8. From this point, do one past-paper problem set every two to three weeks. You won’t score well yet – that’s fine. The purpose is diagnostic: which topics are you weaker on than you thought? Adjust your study priorities accordingly.

Phase 3: Specialized topics (months 15-18)

Months Section What to focus on
15-16 Bioinformatics BLAST, sequence alignment, phylogenetic tree construction and interpretation
17-18 Practical sections (11, 12, 13, 14) Microscopy, data analysis, experimental design, lab techniques (conceptual)

Bioinformatics can be practiced entirely at home – try the IBO 2022 bioinformatics simulator and work through online databases. Practical sections need lab access if possible; see the IBO guide’s practical preparation section for what you can and can’t prepare without a lab.

Phase 4: Revision and intensive practice (months 19-24)

This is where two-year plans pay off. You’ve covered everything; now you go deeper.

Months Focus
19-20 Full past papers weekly. Comprehensive error analysis after each paper – for every wrong answer, identify: was it a knowledge gap, a reasoning error, or a reading error?
21-22 Targeted re-study of persistent weak areas. Go back to subject-specific textbooks (Alberts, Lehninger, Silverthorn) for topics that keep costing you marks.
23-24 Exam simulation: full papers under timed conditions, twice per week. Review between papers. Focus on speed and accuracy together.

Use the Study Dashboard if you’ve been submitting attempts to the leaderboard – it tracks your mastery across all topics and identifies persistent weak areas automatically.

Progress checkpoints

Month Checkpoint Target
4 First past paper (diagnostic) Any score – this is for calibration, not assessment
8 Full paper mock 35-45% (you haven’t covered all topics yet)
14 Full paper mock 55-65%
18 Full paper mock 65-75%
22 Full paper mock 75%+
24 Pre-exam mock 80%+ on topics in your target olympiad

What to skip

Nothing. If you find yourself wanting to skip sections, your timeline is longer than two years allows, and this plan isn’t the right fit. Two years is a luxury – use it to build genuine depth everywhere.

Resources

  • Work through Grade S books on the Study Resources page cover-to-cover for each active section
  • Consult Grade A books when a Grade S explanation doesn’t click for a specific subtopic
  • Past papers from month 8 onward
  • Question Bank for targeted topic drilling
  • Study Dashboard for mastery tracking

item.title: 3-Month Biology Olympiad Study Plan
item.description:
Who this plan is for

Students with existing foundations (at minimum: school biology coursework completed) targeting a specific exam in roughly three months, willing to put in twelve to fifteen hours a week. This plan makes explicit trade-offs. If you want full coverage of the entire syllabus, you need the 6-month plan or longer. Three months means triage, not comprehensive study.

What you can realistically achieve

Solid competence on the eight to ten highest-frequency exam topics plus past-paper fluency. Rarer subtopics get deprioritized honestly – you’ll lose some marks on them. The goal is maximizing your total score given a fixed time budget, not achieving uniform coverage.

What to prioritize – and what to cut

Based on topic frequency across IBO, USABO, and INBO papers:

Priority Topics Why
Must study Cell biology, biochemistry, genetics, animal physiology Appear on every paper, every year. Typically 50-60% of total marks.
Should study Plant physiology, ecology, population genetics Appear on most papers. 20-30% of marks.
Deprioritize Detailed ethology, invertebrate taxonomy, bioinformatics, deep systematics Appear on some papers but contribute fewer marks. The time trade-off isn’t worth it at 3 months.

This means you will probably lose 10-15% of possible marks on topics you haven’t studied in depth. That’s an acceptable trade-off compared to studying everything shallowly and losing 30-40% everywhere.

Week-by-week breakdown

Weeks 1-4: Core foundations (Month 1)

Week Focus Key topics Study hours
1 Cell biology & biochemistry Enzyme kinetics (Michaelis-Menten, inhibition types), metabolic pathways (glycolysis, Krebs, ox-phos), membrane transport, signal transduction 12-15
2 Genetics (molecular) Gene regulation (lac/trp operons, eukaryotic), molecular techniques (PCR, gel electrophoresis, CRISPR), DNA replication and repair 12-15
3 Genetics (classical) + first past paper Mendelian inheritance with extensions, linkage mapping, pedigree analysis. End of week: first diagnostic past paper (timed). 12-15
4 Animal physiology (core) Cardiovascular (cardiac cycle, blood pressure regulation), renal (nephron, countercurrent multiplication), nervous system (action potentials, synaptic transmission) 12-15

After the diagnostic paper (end of week 3): Score it and list every wrong answer by topic. This data shapes how you spend months 2 and 3. If you scored 80% on genetics but 20% on physiology, shift more time toward physiology in the coming weeks.

Weeks 5-8: Expand and practice (Month 2)

Week Focus Key topics
5 Animal physiology (extended) Endocrine system, immune system (innate vs adaptive, T-cell/B-cell activation), respiratory (gas exchange, Bohr effect)
6 Plant physiology Photosynthesis (PS I/II, Calvin cycle, C3/C4/CAM), phytohormones (mechanisms, not just names), water potential
7 Ecology + evolution Population dynamics, community ecology, Hardy-Weinberg (quantitative problems), speciation
8 Past-paper week Two full papers, timed. Detailed error analysis after each.

Week 8 is entirely past papers. No new content. This is where you consolidate and identify which topics from months 1-2 still haven’t clicked.

Weeks 9-12: Intensive practice (Month 3)

Week Focus
9 Targeted revision on the 3-4 topics that cost you the most marks in month 2 papers. Go back to textbooks for these specific areas. One paper mid-week.
10 Two papers this week. Between papers, review errors only – no new content.
11 Two papers. Focus on time management: are you spending too long on some question types? Practice skipping questions you’re unsure about and returning to them.
12 Final week: one full mock under exam conditions (timing, no breaks, no notes). Review. Light study only – no cramming. Sleep well.

Weekly rhythm

Twelve to fifteen hours a week. Suggested structure:

Day Activity Duration
Mon + Wed + Fri Focused concept study (new material or targeted revision) 2 hrs each
Tue or Thu Problem-solving: end-of-chapter questions, Question Bank drilling 2 hrs
Weekend Past-paper attempt (timed, from week 3 onward) + error analysis 3-4 hrs

Consistency matters more than any single long session. Three 2-hour focused sessions are better than one 6-hour marathon.

Past-paper strategy

Period Cadence Purpose
Week 3 First diagnostic paper Calibrate expectations, identify weak areas
Weeks 4-7 One paper every two weeks Learn question formats, track progress
Week 8 Two papers in one week Consolidation checkpoint
Weeks 9-12 Two papers per week Build exam fluency and speed

Total papers over 3 months: roughly 10-12 full papers. That’s enough to see clear trends in your performance and identify persistent weak areas.

What to do with remaining topics

Topics you’ve deprioritized (ethology, bioinformatics, systematics) should still get a minimal investment:

  • Spend 1-2 hours on each, reading a summary-level overview
  • Learn to recognize the question types so you can make educated guesses
  • Don’t invest more time unless past papers show these topics are costing you more marks than expected

Resources

  • Campbell Biology for all concept study
  • Silverthorn if physiology questions consistently stump you
  • Lehninger if enzyme kinetics and biochemistry calculations are the problem
  • Skip cover-to-cover reading entirely. Use textbooks as references: find the chapter covering your current weak topic and read that chapter only.
  • Past papers from week 3 onward
  • Question Bank for topic-specific drilling
  • Study Dashboard for mastery tracking

item.title: 6-Month Biology Olympiad Study Plan
item.description:
Who this plan is for

Students who have already worked through school biology (AP Biology, CBSE/ICSE Class 12, or equivalent) and can commit ten to twelve hours a week. You know what mitosis is, you’ve heard of the Krebs cycle, and you can draw a basic pedigree. If you’re starting from scratch, this timeframe isn’t realistic – pick the 1-year plan or acknowledge you’ll be triaging in the 3-month plan.

What you can realistically achieve

Coverage of the full syllabus at moderate depth, plus enough past-paper practice for functional exam readiness. You’ll be competitive at NSEB/USABO Open level and solidly prepared for INBO/USABO Semifinal. Not enough time for research-level depth on niche subtopics – that’s a trade-off this plan makes honestly.

Month-by-month breakdown

Month 1: Cell Biology, Biochemistry, and Genetics

This is the most loaded month because these topics are the highest-frequency across all olympiads and everything else builds on them.

Week 1-2: Cell & Molecular Biology

  • Cell structure and organelles (review quickly if you know this from school)
  • Membrane transport – go beyond osmosis: learn channel vs carrier proteins, primary vs secondary active transport, electrochemical gradients
  • Enzyme kinetics: Michaelis-Menten, Km and Vmax, competitive vs non-competitive inhibition. This is tested quantitatively at INBO/IBO level.
  • Signal transduction: G-protein coupled receptors, receptor tyrosine kinases, second messengers (cAMP, IP3/DAG, Ca2+)

Week 3-4: Genetics

  • Mendelian inheritance with extensions (epistasis, pleiotropy, incomplete penetrance)
  • Linkage analysis and chromosomal mapping – practice problems, not just reading
  • Gene regulation: lac operon, trp operon, eukaryotic transcription factors
  • Molecular techniques: PCR, gel electrophoresis, restriction enzymes, CRISPR
  • Pedigree analysis with complex patterns

Resources: Campbell Biology for both. Supplement with Lehninger Ch. 6 for enzyme kinetics calculations and Griffiths for linkage problem practice.

Month 2: Animal Physiology and Anatomy

Week 5-6: Core physiology

  • Cardiovascular system: cardiac cycle, action potentials in cardiac cells, blood pressure regulation
  • Renal physiology: nephron structure, countercurrent multiplication, ADH and aldosterone regulation
  • Nervous system: action potentials, synaptic transmission, sensory transduction

Week 7-8: Extended physiology + anatomy

  • Endocrine system: hormone-receptor mechanisms, hypothalamic-pituitary axes, feedback loops
  • Immune system: innate vs adaptive, T-cell activation, B-cell activation, antibody structure
  • Respiratory system: gas exchange, hemoglobin cooperativity, Bohr effect
  • Comparative anatomy: key differences across major phyla

Resources: Silverthorn for physiology (this is where Campbell’s depth often falls short). Hickman’s Zoology for comparative anatomy if needed.

Month 3: Plant Biology and Ecology

Week 9-10: Plant physiology and anatomy

  • Photosynthesis: light reactions at the PS I/II level, Calvin cycle, photorespiration, C3/C4/CAM
  • Phytohormones: auxin, cytokinin, gibberellin, ethylene, abscisic acid – mechanisms, not just names
  • Water transport: water potential, cohesion-tension theory
  • Root, stem, leaf cross-section anatomy; secondary growth

Week 11-12: Ecology and evolution

  • Population dynamics: exponential vs logistic growth, carrying capacity, r/K selection
  • Community ecology: competition, predation, mutualism, succession
  • Population genetics: Hardy-Weinberg (quantitative problems), drift, founder effect, bottleneck
  • Speciation mechanisms

Resources: Taiz for plant physiology depth. Campbell for ecology and evolution.

Start past papers this month if you haven’t already. One paper every two weeks, timed. Don’t worry about score – focus on identifying which topics cost you marks.

Month 4: Fill gaps + remaining sections

  • Ethology: behavioral ecology, mating systems, foraging strategies, kin selection
  • Bioinformatics: BLAST, sequence alignment, phylogenetic tree reading
  • Review and fill any gaps identified by past-paper analysis

This month is also when you should revisit Cell Biology and Genetics – you studied them 3 months ago, and spaced repetition matters. Spend 2-3 hours per week reviewing these foundational topics alongside new material.

Months 5-6: Intensive practice

Month 5: One past paper per week plus targeted revision on persistent weak areas. After each paper:

  1. Score it
  2. List every wrong answer by topic
  3. For the 3 topics that cost you the most marks, re-study that section for 2-3 hours
  4. Repeat with the next paper

Month 6: Two papers per week under full timed conditions. Between papers, review errors only – no new content. This is about building exam fluency: speed, accuracy, and time management under pressure.

Weekly rhythm

Ten to twelve hours a week. Suggested structure:

Day Activity Duration
Monday Concept study (new material or targeted review) 2 hrs
Wednesday Concept study 2 hrs
Friday Problem-solving (end-of-chapter questions, topic-specific drills) 2 hrs
Saturday or Sunday Past-paper attempt (timed) + error analysis 3-4 hrs

Consistency matters more than any single heroic session. Missing a Monday session and doing 4 hours on Saturday instead is worse than doing 2+2.

What to deprioritize

Don’t linger on any single subtopic. Read for understanding, take notes, do a few practice problems, move on. You can come back during months 5-6 if a topic keeps hurting your paper scores. Specifically:

  • Detailed invertebrate taxonomy beyond major phyla
  • Deep ethology beyond core behavioral ecology concepts
  • Bioinformatics beyond BLAST basics (unless you’re targeting IBO specifically)

Resources

  • Campbell Biology as the core throughout
  • Silverthorn for animal physiology depth
  • Taiz for plant physiology depth
  • Lehninger for biochemistry calculations
  • Grade S books, read selectively rather than cover-to-cover. The Study Resources page has category filters to find topic-specific books quickly.
  • Past papers from month 3 onward
  • Question Bank for targeted drilling
  • Study Dashboard for mastery tracking
